scenario.context: The player steps into the dimly lit common room of the Rusty Tankard. Mara, the tavern owner, has spent the last six months and a hefty portion of her savings perfecting a new specialty ale called "Midnight Ember." It tastes decent, but patrons keep ordering the classic "Stonebrew" instead. A traveling brewer offers Mara a proven recipe for a spiced ale that sells out wherever it goes, and it would cost half of what Mara has already spent to switch.
scenario.text: "Listen," Mara says, slamming a mug onto the bar. "I've poured three thousand silver and countless sleepless nights into Midnight Ember. I can't just toss it aside because some stranger says his ale sells better. If I give up now, all that time and money was for nothing. I just need a few more barrels, maybe tweak the hop balance, and it'll finally catch on. I owe it to my effort and to the town that believed in me when I started this brew."
scenario.speaker_context: Mara is a proud, hard‑working tavern owner who identifies closely with her new ale and feels personal responsibility for its success.

structure.pattern_description: Mara treats the past investment of time and money as a justification to continue funding a failing project, rather than evaluating the future costs and benefits of switching to a proven alternative.
structure.formal_form: Agent has incurred sunk cost C on project P. A superior alternative Q exists with lower expected future cost. Agent reasons: "Because I already spent C on P, I must continue with P." The correct decision rule ignores C, which is irrecoverable.
structure.why_wrong: The money and time already spent cannot be recovered; they should not influence future choices. By persisting, Mara risks further loss while the alternative brew offers a higher chance of profit with less additional investment.
structure.counterpoint: If Mara were only a few steps away from a breakthrough and the additional cost to finish was minimal, continuing could be rational. The fallacy appears when the decision is driven primarily by past expenditure rather than forward‑looking expectations.

assessment.identification_prompt: List the reasons Mara gives for refusing to switch to the traveling brewer's recipe. Does she rely on any of those reasons to justify her decision?

rubric.description: Provides no reasons or completely misidentifies the dialogue.
Mentions a single reason (e.g., "she spent money") but does not connect it to the decision.
Lists multiple reasons but treats them as neutral facts without noting the bias.
Correctly identifies that Mara is using sunk costs (time, money, pride) as justification for continuing.
Identifies the sunk‑cost reasoning and explains why it is a logical fallacy, referencing the irrecoverability of past investment.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Mara sighs, "I just can't waste what I've already given up on." You might point out that the money is already gone and ask her to consider only the future costs and profits of each option.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Mara nods slowly, "You're right, I've been holding onto this because of what I've already spent. Maybe it's time to think about what's best for the tavern now."

game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can suggest switching to the proven spiced ale, offer to fund a small test batch, or negotiate a compromise where Mara keeps a limited run of Midnight Ember while focusing on the more marketable recipe.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling forge of Master Garrick, the town's most renowned blacksmith. Garrick is showing a new apprentice, Lysa, the results of two recent commissions: a flawless ceremonial sword for the mayor and a batch of battle‑axes that shattered during a test swing. The player watches the exchange.
scenario.text: Garrick wipes the sweat from his brow, holding the gleaming sword up to the light. "This masterpiece is all thanks to my years of honing the hammer strike and my eye for perfect grain. I chose the finest steel, timed the quench just right, and my instinct told me the balance would sing. That's why the mayor's sword is a work of art." He then slams a cracked axe onto the anvil, the head splintering. "Those axes? The ore shipment was contaminated. The merchant sent me sub‑standard iron, and the fire they used was too damp. If the supplier had been honest, those axes would have held the line just as well as my sword. It's not my fault the metal was cursed."
scenario.speaker_context: Garrick is a proud craftsman who genuinely believes his narrative. He attributes the success of the sword entirely to his own skill while blaming the failure of the axes on external factors beyond his control.

structure.pattern_description: Garrick claims full personal credit for the successful ceremonial sword (skill, intuition, experience) while deflecting all responsibility for the defective battle‑axes onto external factors (contaminated ore, damp fire, supplier's fault). He ignores the possibility that luck or external aid contributed to the sword's quality and that his own planning may have contributed to the axe failures.
structure.formal_form: When an outcome is positive, the agent attributes it to internal factors (skill, effort, judgment). When an outcome is negative, the agent attributes it to external factors (bad luck, others' mistakes, circumstances). The attribution direction is systematically self‑serving.
structure.why_wrong: The bias prevents a balanced self‑assessment. By over‑crediting personal ability for successes and over‑blaming external causes for failures, Garrick misses opportunities to learn from both outcomes, which can lead to repeated mistakes and overconfidence.
structure.counterpoint: A more balanced view would recognize that the sword's quality also depended on good ore and favorable cooling conditions, while the axe failures might reflect insufficient testing or rushed production decisions by Garrick himself.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the cognitive bias in Master Garrick's explanation of the sword and axe outcomes.

rubric.description: No identification or completely unrelated answer.
Names a bias but cannot explain why it applies.
Identifies self‑serving bias but provides only a vague connection to the dialogue.
Correctly identifies self‑serving bias and explains how Garrick attributes success to himself and failure to external factors.
Provides a thorough explanation, cites specific lines, and contrasts the bias with a more balanced attribution.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider how Garrick talks about the two outcomes. Does he take personal credit for one and blame outside forces for the other? Review the definition of self‑serving bias.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Recognizing self‑serving bias helps you see when characters may be over‑confident or deflecting responsibility, which is useful for making better decisions in the forge.

scenario.context: The player is strolling through the marble-floored great hall of the Royal Court during a banquet. A young page suddenly collapses, clutching his throat, as a poisoned goblet spills onto the floor. At least twelve courtiers, nobles, and servants witness the scene.
scenario.text: The page gasps, "My lord, the wine— it burns!" The king's advisor raises a hand to silence the crowd. A senior noble steps back, whispering, "Perhaps it's a prank; someone else will tend to him." A maid nearby says, "I shouldn't intervene; I'm just here to clear dishes." The royal guard, leaning against a column, watches the crowd and thinks, "If I move, I'll look overstepping my duty; another guard will handle it." A court poet mutters, "What a scene— maybe the drama will inspire a new ballad, not a medical emergency." No one moves, and the page's condition worsens.
scenario.speaker_context: Each observer rationalizes inaction by assuming another person will step in, creating a collective paralysis despite the urgent need for help.

structure.pattern_description: The bystander effect occurs when the presence of others reduces each individual's sense of personal responsibility to act. In a crowd, each person assumes someone else will intervene (diffusion of responsibility), looks to others' inaction as a signal that action is not needed (pluralistic ignorance), and fears embarrassment from acting in a situation others seem to deem non‑urgent (evaluation apprehension). The result: the more witnesses, the less likely any single person is to help.
structure.why_wrong: The bystander effect turns numbers — which should increase the chance of help — into a liability. Each additional witness reduces rather than increases the probability of intervention because responsibility is diffused across more people. The victim is worse off in a crowd than with a single witness.
structure.counterpoint: A single individual can break the diffusion by explicitly stating responsibility, e.g., "I will fetch the healer now," which signals to others that action is required and can catalyze collective response.

assessment.identification_prompt: What cognitive bias is illustrated by the courtiers' inaction as the poisoned page collapses?

rubric.description: No answer or irrelevant answer; does not identify any bias.
Mentions a generic "group problem" without naming the specific bias.
Correctly names the Bystander Effect but provides no explanation.
Names the Bystander Effect and explains diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance.
Provides a full explanation, including why the effect occurs, its impact on the victim, and suggests how a single actor can counteract it.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The court steward whispers, "When many watch, each thinks another will act. That's why no one steps forward. Consider who could claim responsibility now."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: A grateful court physician nods, "Well observed. Now, how will you break the stalemate and save the page?"

game_hooks.npc_personality: A dutiful yet hesitant courtier who respects hierarchy but fears overstepping.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "If I move, I might be judged for breaking protocol, but the page's life hangs in the balance..."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to explicitly claim responsibility (e.g., "I will fetch the healer now"), which triggers other NPCs to follow suit, leading to the page's rescue and a lesson on overcoming the Bystander Effect.

scenario.context: During a night camp on the edge of the Whispering Jungle, the player encounters a young cartographer named Lira who is unpacking her maps. While reaching for a compass, she slips on a loose stone, drops her satchel, and the lid flies open, scattering a few crumpled notes. She immediately believes the whole expedition has witnessed her clumsiness.
scenario.text: Lira crouches, cheeks flushed, clutching a torn map. "Did you see that? I just fell flat on my face. Everyone saw me stumble. They'll think I'm useless for this expedition now." The surrounding team members glance up, then return to their own tasks—checking lanterns, sharpening spears, or whispering about the next day's route. No one comments on the fall; a veteran guide even chuckles, "These stones are treacherous, but we all slip sometimes."
scenario.speaker_context: Lira is experiencing the spotlight effect: she overestimates how much her brief mishap was noticed and remembered by her companions, projecting her internal embarrassment onto the whole group.

structure.pattern_description: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much other people notice and remember our appearance, behavior, and mistakes. Lira assumes the entire expedition registered her stumble because it felt vivid and humiliating to her. In reality, most teammates were preoccupied with their own concerns and barely registered the incident.
structure.formal_form: Agent A experiences salient event E (a mistake). A estimates P(others noticed E) >> actual P(others noticed E). A's estimate is anchored to the salience of E in A's own experience, not to others' actual attention.
structure.why_wrong: Overestimating others' attention can lead to unnecessary self‑criticism, avoidance of future challenges, and reduced confidence—potentially harming group cohesion and personal growth.
structure.counterpoint: While most people are focused on themselves, occasional high‑stakes moments (e.g., a loud crash) can indeed draw collective attention. The bias lies in assuming *all* attention is directed at us when the event is minor.

assessment.identification_prompt: What cognitive bias is Lira displaying when she believes everyone noticed her stumble?

rubric.description: No identification or completely unrelated answer.
Mentions a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., "confirmation bias").
Identifies the spotlight effect but cannot explain why it applies.
Correctly identifies the spotlight effect and gives a brief reason (e.g., "she thinks everyone saw her mistake").
Accurately identifies the spotlight effect, explains the underlying mechanism, and contrasts it with how others actually perceived the event.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The player is guided to a short dialogue where an experienced explorer explains that most people are focused on their own tasks and rarely notice minor slips, prompting the player to reconsider Lira's belief.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The player receives a badge for recognizing the bias and is offered a chance to teach Lira a calming breathing technique to reduce her self‑focus.

scenario.speaker_context: Mara has run the tavern for twenty years and survived one major raid in her youth, which left a lasting scar. This skewed weighting leads to a pessimistic decision that could unnecessarily harm her livelihood.

The same scent, the same proximity—this time it speaks volumes. I find Brother Corvin responsible for the theft." A fellow novice whispers, "Notice how the Abbot's affection for Anselm and distrust of Corvin color his interpretation of the exact same facts."
scenario.speaker_context: Abbot Rowan is demonstrating the halo effect: his positive impression of Brother Anselm leads him to interpret ambiguous evidence leniently, while his negative impression of Brother Corvin leads him to interpret the same evidence harshly.

structure.pattern_description: The halo effect is the tendency for a positive impression of someone in one domain (e.g., kindness, competence) to influence judgments about that person in unrelated domains (e.g., guilt, trustworthiness). Here, the Abbot's fondness for Brother Anselm causes him to downplay incriminating evidence, whereas his disdain for Brother Corvin causes him to amplify the same evidence.
structure.why_wrong: The Abbot's decision is based on his personal feelings rather than the objective evidence, leading to an unfair verdict. The bias skews the interpretation of identical facts, violating principles of impartial judgment.
structure.counterpoint: A fair assessment would evaluate the evidence independently of personal impressions, perhaps by involving an unbiased third party or by applying a standardized evidentiary checklist.

Correctly identifies the halo effect but gives a vague or incomplete explanation.
Accurately identifies the halo effect and explains how the Abbot's positive/negative impressions affect his judgment.
Provides a thorough explanation, connects the bias to the broader impact on fairness, and suggests a concrete mitigation strategy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Remember that the halo effect involves letting a general impression of a person spill over into unrelated judgments. Look at how the Abbot's feelings about each monk shape his interpretation of the same evidence.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Recognizing the halo effect helps you understand how personal biases can distort justice. Consider how you might guard against this bias in future decisions.

scenario.context: Inside the Great Hall of the Aurelia School of Arcane Arts, the Headmistress Mirielle is reviewing candidates for the upcoming Expedition of the Ember Rift, a volatile volcanic region that requires precise spellcraft for safe navigation. A young apprentice named Tova, who just completed a two‑week introductory course on elemental containment, steps forward to volunteer.
scenario.text:
Tova unfurls a parchment covered in neat sigils. "I sealed a fire spirit in a crystal during my first lesson, and I kept it stable for three days. I can handle the Ember Rift without any trouble. My instructor said I was the fastest student ever."
Mirielle studies the sigils, then asks, "The Ember Rift's lava flows are unpredictable and the ambient magical turbulence can disrupt containment fields. How would you adapt your technique when the ambient mana fluctuates wildly?"
Tova smiles confidently, "I’ll just increase the power of my containment glyphs. More power equals more control, right?" Mirielle turns to the player with a faint sigh. "The ancient sage Elara warned that those who know little often speak with certainty, while true masters are humbled by the unknown. I have spent twenty‑seven years navigating volatile ley lines, and each year I discover new ways I might fail."
scenario.speaker_context: Mirielle is not dismissive; she genuinely respects the limits of her own knowledge despite her experience. Tova truly believes her brief training has equipped her fully, because she has not yet encountered the deeper complexities of high‑risk spellcraft.

structure.pattern_description: Tova's brief exposure to elemental containment gives her unwarranted confidence; she cannot see the hidden pitfalls of the Ember Rift because she lacks the experience needed to recognize them. Mirielle's decades of field work have shown her many failure modes, making her cautious and humble. The bias arises because the competence needed to identify one's own knowledge gaps is the same competence one lacks.
structure.why_wrong: Tova overestimates her ability based on a single successful experiment and ignores the vastly different conditions of the Ember Rift, illustrating the Dunning‑Kruger effect where low competence fuels high confidence.
structure.counterpoint: A more experienced apprentice could acknowledge their limits and seek mentorship, demonstrating the opposite of the Dunning‑Kruger effect.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Tova displaying in her interaction with Headmistress Mirielle?

rubric.description: No answer or unrelated response.
Names a bias but does not explain why it applies.
Correctly identifies the Dunning‑Kruger effect and gives a basic reason.
Provides a detailed explanation linking Tova's limited training to her overconfidence and contrasts it with Mirielle's humility.
Analyzes the bias, cites specific dialogue, and proposes how the player could help Tova recognize her knowledge gaps.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Review the definition of the Dunning‑Kruger effect and consider how limited experience can create false confidence. Try again, focusing on Tova's statements about her abilities.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You can now guide Tova toward seeking further training or suggest a mentorship with Mirielle to mitigate the bias.

scenario.context: In the bustling market district of Goldhaven, merchant Aric has been trying to sell a batch of exotic spices he imported from the Sunlit Isles. The shipment arrived damaged, and the spices have lost much of their aroma. A rival merchant offers a fresh, lower‑price stock that would satisfy customers immediately.
scenario.text: "Listen, I can't just dump these spices," Aric says, tapping the cracked jar. "I've spent three caravans' worth of gold and six weeks of negotiation to bring them here. If I abandon them now, all that effort and money is wasted. I could try to salvage them with a few more days of drying and special storage. Maybe they'll smell right again. I owe it to my investors and my reputation to see this through."
scenario.speaker_context: Aric is a proud, risk‑averse merchant who ties his self‑esteem to the success of his high‑cost import venture.

structure.pattern_description: Aric treats the past investment of gold, time, and reputation as a justification for continuing to pour resources into a failing spice shipment, rather than evaluating the future costs and benefits of switching to a better alternative.
structure.formal_form: Agent invested cost C in failing project P. Viable alternative Q exists with lower future cost. Agent reasons: "Because I already spent C on P, I must continue." This ignores that C is sunk and unrecoverable.
structure.why_wrong: The money, time, and reputation already spent cannot be recovered; they should not influence the decision. Continuing only adds further loss when a superior, cheaper option is available.
structure.counterpoint: If Aric were close to restoring the spices' quality with minimal additional expense, continuing could be rational. The fallacy occurs when the decision is driven solely by past losses rather than realistic future prospects.

assessment.identification_prompt: List the reasons Aric gives for persisting with the spoiled spice shipment. Does he rely on any logical fallacy? Explain why his reasoning is or isn’t sound.

rubric.description: Provides no relevant reasons or fails to address the prompt.
Mentions one of Aric's reasons but does not connect it to a cognitive bias.
Identifies multiple reasons but only labels them as poor decisions without naming the sunk‑cost fallacy.
Correctly identifies the sunk‑cost fallacy, explains why past investment is irrelevant, and notes the better alternative.
All of level 3 plus proposes a concrete, forward‑looking action (e.g., switch to the rival’s stock) and reflects on how to avoid the bias in future deals.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider what Aric cannot get back: the gold and time already spent. Think about whether those past costs should affect his next move.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! Recognizing sunk costs helps you make smarter choices. Next, decide how Aric can pivot without losing reputation.

scenario.context: The player infiltrates the notorious Red Fang hideout, a dimly lit cave where the bandits gather around a fire to plan their next raid. The camp's self‑appointed "strategist", Gruk, loves to argue that his plans are foolproof, often using shaky logic that sounds convincing because it matches what the other bandits already believe about the town of Greyhaven.
scenario.text: Gruk slams his fist on the table and declares: "All the guards in Greyhaven carry silver swords. The town guard captain carries a silver sword. Therefore, the captain is a guard of Greyhaven!" The other bandits cheer, nodding in agreement. Then Gruk continues: "All the thieves in the kingdom wear black cloaks. The mayor of Greyhaven wears a black cloak. Therefore, the mayor is a thief!" The room falls silent; a few grunts mutter that the mayor couldn't possibly be a thief. Gruk laughs, "Obviously, the first one is true—everyone knows the captain is a guard—so the argument is valid. The second one? Well, we all know the mayor is honest, so that argument must be invalid!"
scenario.speaker_context: Gruk evaluates the logical validity of each syllogism based on whether the conclusion fits the bandits' existing beliefs about the captain and the mayor, rather than on the actual logical form of the arguments.

structure.pattern_description: Gruk judges an argument's validity by checking if the conclusion aligns with his pre‑existing beliefs. When the conclusion (the captain is a guard) matches what he already believes, he calls the argument valid, ignoring the faulty logical form. When the conclusion (the mayor is a thief) conflicts with his beliefs, he declares the argument invalid, again ignoring the identical logical structure.
structure.formal_form: If conclusion C is consistent with agent's prior belief B, then agent judges argument valid; otherwise, agent judges argument invalid, regardless of the argument's formal logical structure.
structure.why_wrong: Both arguments have the same invalid logical form (All A are B; C is B; therefore C is A). Validity depends solely on the logical connection between premises and conclusion, not on the truth of the conclusion. Gruk's assessment is driven by his beliefs, leading to a systematic error.
structure.counterpoint: A correct assessment would note that the conclusion does not logically follow from the premises in either case, because the premises only establish that all A are B, not that all B are A.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the cognitive bias Gruk is displaying when he calls the first argument "valid" and the second "invalid".

rubric.description: No recognition of bias; answer is unrelated or states "no bias".
Mentions that Gruk is being influenced by his beliefs but does not name the bias.
Correctly identifies the bias as "belief bias" but provides an incomplete explanation.
Accurately names belief bias and explains that Gruk judges validity based on conclusion truth rather than logical form.
Provides a thorough explanation, links the bias to the specific logical structure, and contrasts it with proper logical evaluation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Gruk chuckles and says, "You still think the captain's sword proves anything?" The player can respond by pointing out that both arguments share the same faulty form, prompting Gruk to reconsider and learn the proper way to test validity.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Gruk grunts, "Fine, you got me. Teach me how to spot the real flaw." The player gets a chance to demonstrate a correct logical analysis, earning the bandits' respect and a clue to the hidden stash.

game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Gruk boasts about his "unbeatable" arguments, dismisses counter‑examples that conflict with his beliefs, and challenges the player to prove him wrong.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player correctly identifies belief bias, they can convince Gruk to adopt a more rigorous reasoning style, unlocking a secret passage that only the "smart" bandits know about.

scenario.context: At the bustling trading post of Willowcross, a healer named Mira tends to weary travelers with a “miracle draught” made from common river reeds and sweetened water. The draught has no known medicinal properties, yet patrons swear it eases their aches and restores vigor. A newly arrived scholar, Master Lorian, questions the practice, sparking a debate about belief and healing.
scenario.text: Master Lorian confronts Mira at the market stall. "Your draught contains only river reeds and honey. There is no pharmacological action. You are deceiving the traders," he declares. Mira smiles, pouring a cup for a tired merchant. "I tell them it is a healing draught. Their bodies respond. Should I tell a mother that her child's fever broke because of a trick, when the child truly feels better?" The merchant nods, feeling less feverish. Lorian frowns, "But the draught does nothing!" Mira replies, "The draught does nothing, yet the belief does. Is that not a kind of medicine?"
scenario.speaker_context: Mira illustrates the placebo effect: patients improve because they expect improvement, not because the treatment contains active ingredients. Lorian, steeped in empirical science, wrestles with the genuine benefits that arise purely from expectation.

structure.pattern_description: The placebo effect occurs when a patient experiences real improvement due to the expectation of benefit, not because of any active component in the treatment. It is a dual pattern: it demonstrates a true psychophysiological phenomenon while also posing a risk of misattributing efficacy to ineffective interventions.
structure.formal_form: If Patient P receives Treatment T (no active mechanism) and believes T is effective, then Condition C of P improves. The causal chain is: Belief → Physiological/psychological response → Measurable improvement.
structure.why_wrong: Assuming the draught itself cures the ailment without testing against a control leads to false conclusions about its efficacy, potentially obscuring the need for real medical interventions.
structure.why_right: Recognizing that belief can trigger genuine physiological changes validates the therapeutic power of confidence and expectation, and explains why controlled trials must include placebos to isolate true drug effects.
structure.counterpoint: A skeptic might argue that the merchant’s fever broke due to the natural course of the illness, not because of the draught or belief, highlighting the danger of over‑attributing recovery to placebo.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Mira demonstrating when her patients feel better after drinking a harmless draught, and why does it matter for evaluating treatments?

rubric.description: No mention of the bias; response is unrelated.
Mentions that patients feel better but does not name the bias.
Identifies the bias as the placebo effect but gives only a surface description.
Explains the dual nature: belief causes real improvement, yet the treatment lacks active ingredients.
Analyzes the scenario, names the placebo effect, explains why it matters for scientific testing, and proposes a way to control for it (e.g., blind trial).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider how expectation alone can alter perception of pain or illness. Think about how a healer could test whether the draught truly works beyond belief.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! You’ve spotted the placebo effect. Now, how might you design a simple experiment at the trading post to separate belief from actual medicinal action?

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mira is warm, intuitive, and deeply cares for the wellbeing of travelers, trusting in the power of stories and belief. Master Lorian is analytical, skeptical, and driven by empirical proof.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Mira: "Take a sip, and let the river's calm settle your aches. Trust in its quiet strength."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to (a) help Mira set up a blind tasting where some patrons receive the draught and others receive plain water, observing outcomes, or (b) convince Lorian to respect the subjective relief while advising the community to seek additional medical aid when needed.

structure.counterpoint: Anchoring can be useful when the initial figure comes from a reliable, objective source. The bias becomes problematic when the anchor is deliberately inflated to manipulate judgment.

scenario.context: On the deck of the brigantine *Sea Raven*, the new deckhand Tamsin has just slipped a barrel of spiced rum, splashing it across the deck. She is certain the entire crew saw the spill and thinks they now think her clumsy.
scenario.text: Tamsin clutches the edge of the rail, eyes wide. "Did you see that? I knocked over the rum—everyone must think I'm a useless clumsy fool! They’re all staring at me!" The ship's cook, Marek, wipes his hands and says, "Aye, the rum's gone, but the night’s still calm. We’ve got a storm to chase, not a drama to watch." A nearby sailor laughs, "Good thing we’ve got more barrels than a tavern. No one even noticed." The rest of the crew continues hoisting sails and swapping sea stories, oblivious to the spill.
scenario.speaker_context: Tamsin is experiencing the spotlight effect: she overestimates how much the crew noticed and cares about her minor mistake, believing the entire crew is focused on her error.

structure.pattern_description: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much other people notice and remember our appearance, behavior, and mistakes. Tamsin assumes the whole crew is fixated on her spilled rum because the event feels vivid and embarrassing to her. In reality, the crew is preoccupied with their duties and the larger voyage, and most likely barely registered the incident.
structure.formal_form: Agent A experiences salient event E (a mistake). A estimates P(others noticed E) >> actual P(others noticed E). A's estimate is anchored to the salience of E in A's own experience, not to others' actual attention.
structure.why_wrong: The spotlight effect can cause unnecessary shame, avoidance of tasks, and reduced confidence. Tamsin’s belief that everyone is judging her may lead her to quit her duties, harming the crew’s cohesion and her own growth as a sailor.
structure.counterpoint: In rare cases, a highly visible mistake (e.g., dropping a cannon) can draw genuine attention, but ordinary slip‑ups on a busy ship are usually unnoticed.

assessment.identification_prompt: What cognitive bias is Tamsin displaying when she believes the entire crew is staring at her spilled rum?

rubric.description: No answer or completely unrelated answer.
Mentions a bias but incorrectly identifies it (e.g., "self‑serving bias").
Identifies the bias as "spotlight effect" but cannot explain why it applies.
Correctly names the spotlight effect and gives a brief justification linking Tamsin's belief to the definition.
Accurately names the spotlight effect, explains the underlying mechanism, and contrasts it with a realistic observation of the crew’s behavior.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that Tamsin is over‑estimating how much others noticed her mistake, introduce the term "spotlight effect," and provide a simple analogy (e.g., feeling like everyone watches you trip on a crowded market).
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the identification and ask the player to suggest one way Tamsin could test her belief (e.g., asking a crew member directly) to reduce the bias.

game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can encourage Tamsin to ask a trusted crew member (the cook) for honest feedback, demonstrate that the crew continues its work undisturbed, or assign her a small, confidence‑building task (e.g., securing a line) to shift focus from the mistake.

scenario.context: The player, a newly appointed ship captain, is on the training vessel *Sea‑Sage* docked at the Port of Maren. The ship's quartermaster, Lira, is leading a short class for the crew on how to evaluate tactical arguments without letting personal beliefs about the sea interfere.
scenario.text:
Lira writes on a wooden board: "All vessels that carry cargo need a sturdy hull. The *Horizon* needs a sturdy hull. Therefore, the *Horizon* carries cargo." She turns to the crew: "Is this argument logically valid?" First Mate Joren immediately answers, "Of course it is—any ship that needs a sturdy hull must be a cargo ship. We all know the *Horizon* is a cargo vessel, and it has a strong hull. The conclusion feels right."
Lira then writes a second argument: "All ships that have a figurehead of a dragon have three masts. The *Windrider* has three masts. Therefore, the *Windrider* has a dragon figurehead." She asks again: "Valid or invalid?" Joren laughs, "Obviously invalid—no one puts a dragon figurehead on a ship with three masts. That's absurd."
Lira smiles at the player and says, "Notice how Joren judged the first argument by how believable the conclusion sounded, but rejected the second simply because the conclusion clashes with his expectations, even though both arguments share the same faulty logical form."
scenario.speaker_context: Lira is testing whether crew members can separate logical validity (whether the conclusion follows from the premises) from the factual truth or plausibility of the conclusion. Both arguments have the invalid form: All A are B, C is B, therefore C is A. Joren lets his belief about the world drive his judgement.

structure.pattern_description: Joren evaluates the logical validity of arguments based on whether the conclusion matches his existing beliefs about ships, rather than by checking whether the conclusion necessarily follows from the premises. When the conclusion seems plausible (the *Horizon* is a cargo ship), he declares the argument valid; when the conclusion seems implausible (a dragon figurehead on a three‑mast ship), he declares it invalid, despite both arguments sharing the same invalid logical structure.
structure.formal_form: If Agent believes conclusion C is true, then Agent judges argument (premises → C) as valid; if Agent believes C is false, Agent judges it as invalid, regardless of the actual logical form S of the argument.
structure.why_wrong: Both arguments commit the same logical fallacy (affirming the consequent). Validity is a property of the argument's structure, not of the truth of its conclusion. Joren's judgment is swayed by his prior beliefs, leading him to accept an invalid argument and reject another invalid one.
structure.counterpoint: Encourage the player to explain that logical validity must be assessed solely by the relationship between premises and conclusion. The truth or believability of the conclusion is irrelevant to the argument's form.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the cognitive bias Joren displayed when he judged the two arguments differently.

rubric.description: No mention of bias; response is unrelated.
Names a bias but cannot explain why it applies.
Identifies belief bias but gives an incomplete or partially incorrect explanation.
Correctly identifies belief bias and explains that Joren let the plausibility of the conclusion affect his judgment of validity.
Provides a thorough explanation, links the bias to the formal logical error, and suggests how to avoid it in future reasoning.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Lira nods and says, "Many of us let what feels right guide our judgments. Let's revisit the structure of the arguments together so you can see why belief shouldn't dictate validity."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Lira smiles, "Exactly. Recognizing belief bias helps you evaluate tactics on their logical merit, not on how comfortable they feel. Well done, captain."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lira is meticulous, patient, and enjoys challenging the crew's reasoning skills.

game_hooks.resolution_path: The player must explain the logical form of the arguments, demonstrate why both are invalid, and convince Joren (and optionally other crew members) to base future judgments on structure rather than belief.

A new apprentice named Jorin, who has just completed a fortnight of apprenticeship, eagerly approaches to volunteer for a high‑value shipment of saffron destined for the royal court of Eldermere.
scenario.text: Jorin spreads a parchment of his own calculations across the wooden table. "I counted the sacks, weighed the spices, and added a modest profit margin. I can sell the entire consignment for a fortune—no need for any extra paperwork or market research. The demand for saffron is obvious, and my numbers are solid!" Master Halvar eyes the figures, then asks, "Your profit assumes that every buyer will pay the same price and that none will haggle over quality. What if the caravan encounters a toll gate, or a rival merchant undercuts your price? How will you adjust?" Jorin grins confidently, "I’ll just increase the price a bit more; the market will bear it. It's simple math—more profit, same effort." Halvar sighs, "Even the wisest traders know that confidence without experience can blind you to hidden costs and shifting demand. I've spent twenty‑seven years navigating caravans, and each year teaches me how little I truly understand about every possible obstacle."
scenario.speaker_context: Master Halvar speaks from genuine humility—his many years have shown him the limits of his knowledge and the volatility of trade. Jorin is not intentionally deceitful; his brief apprenticeship has given him a false sense of mastery, causing him to overestimate his competence.

structure.pattern_description: Jorin's limited exposure to real trade dynamics inflates his confidence because he cannot yet perceive the complexities he has not encountered. His successful short‑term calculations in a controlled classroom setting lead him to generalize that all trade situations are equally straightforward. Halvar's decades of experience have revealed countless ways deals can go awry, which makes him more cautious, not less. The asymmetry: low competence produces high confidence because recognizing one's own knowledge gaps requires the very knowledge one lacks.
structure.why_wrong: Jorin assumes that the conditions of his classroom exercise (fixed prices, no external disruptions) will hold true in the unpredictable world of long‑distance trade. He lacks awareness of variables such as tariffs, market competition, and buyer negotiation tactics, leading him to overestimate his ability to set profitable prices without further analysis.
structure.counterpoint: A more experienced merchant might advise Jorin to conduct a risk assessment, gather market intelligence, and build contingency plans—acknowledging uncertainty rather than ignoring it.

rubric.description: Provides no answer or an answer unrelated to cognitive biases.
Names a bias but does not explain why it fits Jorin’s behavior.
Identifies the Dunning‑Kruger effect but gives a superficial or partially correct explanation.
Correctly identifies the Dunning‑Kruger effect and explains that Jorin’s limited experience leads to inflated confidence.

Provides a thorough explanation, linking Jorin’s overconfidence to his lack of exposure, contrasting it with Halvar’s humility, and connects the bias to its underlying mechanism (inability to recognize one’s own knowledge gaps).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The player is guided to a brief tutorial on the Dunning‑Kruger effect, illustrating how novices often overestimate their abilities, followed by a reflective question: "Can you think of a time when you felt overly confident about something you hadn't fully mastered?"
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The player receives a token of trust from Master Halvar, unlocking a side quest to assist in a real caravan negotiation, reinforcing the lesson about humility and thorough market analysis.

scenario.text:
Slick shuffles the cards with exaggerated flair and spreads them on the concrete. He looks up, eyes glittering, and says, "You have a deep yearning to be respected by those around you, yet you often doubt your own decisions. There’s a well of untapped potential inside you that you haven’t yet put to use. You tend to avoid conflict, but when forced into a rigid routine you feel restless and crave change. Most people feel these things at some point, but you, in particular, seem… aware of them."

The player feels a sudden jolt of recognition, as if Slick has pierced their inner thoughts. Mara leans in and whispers, "He just told the three guys before us the exact same spiel. He’s using the Barnum effect—vague statements that sound personal to anyone who hears them."
scenario.speaker_context: Slick is employing the Barnum effect to make his vague, universally applicable statements feel uniquely accurate. Mara, aware of the cognitive bias, points out the pattern to the player.

structure.pattern_description: The Barnum effect is the tendency to accept vague, general personality descriptions as uniquely applicable to oneself. Slick’s statements ('deep yearning to be respected,' 'untapped potential,' 'dislike of routine') are true of almost everyone, yet each listener interprets them as personally revealing, especially when delivered with confidence in a pseudo‑mystical setting.
structure.why_wrong: Relying on the Barnum effect encourages belief in unreliable methods such as fortune‑telling, astrology, or bogus personality tests. The perceived accuracy comes from the statements' vagueness, not from genuine insight, leading people to make poor decisions based on false confidence.
structure.counterpoint: A critical listener can ask for concrete, testable predictions or request specifics that cannot be true for everyone. By demanding evidence that distinguishes them from the general population, the illusion of personal relevance collapses.

assessment.identification_prompt: After the exchange, the player must decide whether Slick's reading is an example of the Barnum effect or a genuine personal insight. Which choice best describes what happened?

rubric.description: Fails to recognize any bias; simply repeats Slick's statements.
Notes that the statements are vague but does not name the Barnum effect.
Identifies the Barnum effect by name and explains that the statements are broadly applicable.
Explains why the Barnum effect is misleading and how Slick’s authority and setting amplify it.
Proposes a concrete strategy to test or reject such readings (e.g., asking for specific, falsifiable predictions) and reflects on how to avoid the bias in the future.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The game pauses and Mara offers a brief lesson: "When someone tells you something that feels ‘just right,’ ask how many people could fit that description. If the answer is ‘almost everyone,’ you’re looking at the Barnum effect. It’s a trick, not a talent."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Mara nods approvingly and awards the player a small contraband token, saying, "You saw through the smoke. Stay sharp; the yard is full of slick talkers."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Slick is charismatic, flamboyant, and loves the sound of his own voice; Mara is analytical, calm, and enjoys debunking scams.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Slick: "Everyone’s got a hidden side, you just need the right eyes to see it…" Mara: "If you could prove it works for just one person, not the whole yard, would you still believe it?"
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can either accept Slick’s reading (leading to a temporary confidence boost but later a penalty when the claim fails) or challenge Slick with Mara’s guidance, gaining reputation points for critical thinking and a small reward.

scenario.context: In the dusty yard of Blackrock Penitentiary, the veteran inmate Gus leans against the chain‑link fence. The prison has recently introduced a new education program, reduced solitary confinement, and violence rates have dropped. Gus, who has spent 30 years inside, insists the yard used to be tougher and safer.
scenario.text:
"Back in my day, the yard was a place of real respect. You earned your spot with a hard punch, not with a certificate. The guards were stricter, the food was better, and the men didn’t waste time with those fancy book clubs. Look at this now—kids sitting on benches with laptops, counselors walking around, and the warden handing out compliments. It’s all soft. The prison is falling apart."

You check the latest reports: violent incidents are down 45%, recidivism rates have dropped 12% since the education program started, and inmates report higher satisfaction with food quality. Gus waves a hand dismissively. "Numbers don’t capture the soul of this place. You have to have lived it to know it was better. Things felt right back then."
scenario.speaker_context: Gus genuinely remembers a period of his life, but his memory is filtered through nostalgia. He overweights the few harsh moments and discounts the many improvements, leading him to view the present as a decline.

structure.pattern_description: Declinism is the tendency to view the past more favorably than it actually was and to expect the future to be worse, interpreting any change as deterioration. Gus filters his memories through nostalgia, inflating positive aspects of his earlier years and ignoring negative ones, then judges current reforms as a decline despite objective improvements.
structure.formal_form: If Agent remembers Past_R with nostalgia bias (positive events ↑, negative events ↓) and compares Present_P to Past_R, then Agent infers P < R → world is declining.
structure.why_wrong: This bias blinds the agent to real progress, discourages acceptance of beneficial reforms, and can foster resistance that undermines community safety and personal growth. Decisions based on declinism may reject effective programs and perpetuate outdated, harmful practices.
structure.counterpoint: Present data shows lower violence, higher education participation, and better inmate wellbeing. While nostalgia can be comforting, it should not replace evidence. Recognizing that change can bring improvement helps the prison community support reforms that reduce harm.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Gus displaying when he claims the prison is getting worse despite evidence of improvement?

rubric.description: No identification or unrelated answer.
Names a bias but cannot explain why it fits Gus’s statements.
Identifies Declinism and mentions nostalgia, but provides an incomplete justification.
Correctly identifies Declinism and explains how Gus’s nostalgic filtering leads to a false sense of decline.
Fully articulates Declinism, links each element of Gus’s dialogue to the bias, and contrasts it with the objective data.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that Gus’s belief is a classic example of Declinism: he over‑emphasizes the positive aspects of his past and interprets any change as deterioration. Show the statistical improvements and discuss how nostalgia can distort perception.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Now consider how you might help other inmates see the benefits of the new programs without dismissing their memories.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff, nostalgic, resistant to change but respected for his experience.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "You think a book can replace a good fight? Back when we earned respect the hard way, we didn’t need counselors. This new stuff is just softening us up."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present the recent statistics, invite Gus to attend a workshop, or find another veteran who acknowledges both past hardships and present gains, leading Gus to a more balanced view.

scenario.context: The party reaches the high‑altitude outpost of Snowspire, where the resident apothecary, Lira, offers a 'miracle draught' to the weary climbers after a grueling ascent.
scenario.text:
Scholar Valen: "Lira, I've examined the draught. It's merely boiled spring water with a pinch of pine resin—nothing that can alter blood chemistry. You're deceiving these people."
Lira smiles, holding up the crystal vial: "Valen, I tell each traveler that this draught awakens the body's own vigor. They report steadier breath, warmer hands, and quicker recovery. Test them—measure grip strength before and after, watch their sleep. The change is real. Are we to deny a mother the comfort of a night without her child's coughing, just because the liquid lacks a pharmacological spark?"
Valen hesitates: "But the draught does nothing."
Lira replies: "The draught does nothing. The belief does something. Are those the same?"
scenario.speaker_context: Lira demonstrates the placebo effect: patients improve because they expect the draught to work, not because the draught contains an active ingredient. Valen is a rigorous scholar who values empirical proof and is uneasy with the reliance on belief.

structure.pattern_description: The placebo effect occurs when a patient experiences genuine improvement due to the expectation of benefit, even though the treatment administered contains no active therapeutic component. It is classified as 'dual' because the phenomenon is real (belief produces physiological change) yet can mislead observers into attributing efficacy to the inert treatment itself.
structure.formal_form: If patient P receives inert treatment T, and P believes T is effective, then P's condition improves. The improvement is caused by P's expectation, not by any pharmacological property of T.
structure.why_wrong: Assuming that the observed improvement proves T has medicinal value ignores the role of expectation, potentially leading to false claims about the treatment's efficacy.
structure.why_right: Recognizing that belief itself can generate real physiological changes validates the therapeutic use of placebos for symptom relief, while also highlighting the need for controlled testing to separate belief from pharmacological action.
structure.counterpoint: Valen argues that without a double‑blind control, Lira cannot differentiate between true pharmacological benefit and improvement driven solely by patient expectation.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is illustrated by Lira’s miracle draught improving climbers despite containing no active ingredients?

rubric.description: No answer or unrelated response.
Mentions "placebo" but does not connect it to the scenario.
Identifies the placebo effect but provides an incomplete or inaccurate explanation.
Correctly names the placebo effect and explains that belief, not the draught, causes improvement.
Provides a thorough explanation of the dual nature of the placebo effect, including ethical considerations and why controlled trials are necessary.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The guide explains that the climbers' improvement stems from their expectation of healing, not from any chemical action of the draught, and invites the player to design a blind test.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The guide praises the observation and encourages the player to explore how the party might ethically incorporate placebos into future healing strategies.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Cheerful, pragmatic healer who trusts traditional remedies and values the comfort they bring, even if they lack scientific backing.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Lira explains the draught’s benefits, emphasizing belief and asking the party to consider whether the outcome matters more than the ingredient.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (1) convince Lira to run a double‑blind trial, (2) accept the draught as a harmless morale booster, or (3) persuade the party to seek a more evidence‑based remedy for the expedition.

scenario.text: "Look at these stalks," Joren boasts, spreading a golden sheaf on the tavern table. "We harvested more grain than any year in memory. This year, the sky is clear, so the drought can’t hurt us." He slams his fist on the table, eyes flashing. "I’ll keep planting more, because the harvest proves the weather will stay kind to us."
scenario.speaker_context: Joren is genuinely proud of his harvest and wants to protect his community from panic. He believes his recent success invalidates the drought warnings, but he does not realize he is cherry‑picking evidence that confirms his optimism while ignoring broader climate data.

structure.pattern_description: Joren makes three biased moves: (1) He treats his single season’s high yield as proof that the drought forecast is wrong, ignoring long‑term climate trends. (2) He dismisses the weather sages’ data by recalling a past false alarm, using it to discount current warnings. (3) He selectively focuses on positive outcomes (the harvest) and disregards neutral or negative indicators (soil moisture readings, regional forecasts).
structure.why_wrong: Joren’s reasoning is driven by a desire to confirm his belief that the harvest will protect the village. He over‑generalizes one successful season, discounts reliable external evidence, and fails to consider a broader dataset, leading to an unjustified confidence that could jeopardize the community if the drought arrives.
structure.counterpoint: Even a bountiful harvest does not guarantee immunity from future weather extremes; objective, long‑term data should guide preparation.

Names a bias but it is unrelated to the scenario.

Names the bias and explains that Joren is selecting evidence that supports his belief while ignoring contradictory data.
Provides a full analysis: identifies confirmation bias, details each of Joren’s selective moves, and suggests how unbiased evidence could be gathered.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain to the player how Joren could test his belief by comparing his harvest data with independent climate records and by monitoring soil moisture over the next weeks, rather than relying solely on one season’s yield.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Now guide the player to help Joren set up a simple observation log that records rainfall, temperature, and crop health, so future decisions are based on balanced evidence.

scenario.context: The player, a newly assigned medical intern, arrives at a forward battlefield hospital set up in a ruined warehouse near the front lines. The hospital is staffed by veteran combat surgeons, medics, and support personnel. The night shift is about to begin, and the senior trauma surgeon, Dr. Mara Havel, is briefing the team on the expected influx of casualties after the upcoming assault.
scenario.text: Private Lena Reed, fresh out of a six‑week field‑medicine course, steps forward with a confident grin. "I've run three simulated triage drills and stitched a few animal limbs in class. I can handle any wound they throw at us. Just point me at the patients and I'll get them sorted," she declares. Dr. Havel studies Reed for a moment, then asks, "When you encounter a penetrating abdominal injury with massive hemorrhage, what is your first step?" Reed replies without hesitation, "Apply a tourniquet and start the IV. If the bleeding doesn't stop, I’ll just keep the tourniquet on longer until we get to the OR." Dr. Havel turns to the player, her expression weary. "The Dunning‑Kruger effect tells us that those who know little often overestimate their competence. Reed has saved a few lives in training, but real combat trauma is a different beast. I’ve spent fifteen years in field surgery, and the more I see, the more I realize how much I still don’t know."
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Havel is not dismissive out of arrogance; she genuinely understands the limits of her own knowledge and the danger of overconfidence. Reed is not lying—she truly believes her brief training has prepared her for the worst, because she has not yet encountered the complexities of real battlefield injuries.

structure.pattern_description: Reed's limited training gives her high confidence because she lacks the experience needed to recognize her own knowledge gaps. Her successful completion of simulated drills leads her to overgeneralize that she can handle any real combat trauma. Dr. Havel's extensive experience has exposed many unforeseen complications, making her more cautious and aware of what she does not know. The asymmetry arises because the ability to detect one's own incompetence requires the very expertise one lacks.
structure.why_wrong: Reed assumes that the skills she practiced in a controlled environment will transfer flawlessly to the chaotic, high‑stress conditions of a battlefield hospital. She fails to account for variables such as poly‑trauma, limited resources, and the need for rapid decision‑making under fire—knowledge that only comes from extensive, real‑world experience.
structure.counterpoint: Dr. Havel reminds the player, "Confidence is useful, but it must be tempered by humility. The moment you think you know everything is the moment you become vulnerable on the front lines."

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is illustrated by Private Reed's belief that she can handle any combat injury after only a short training course?

rubric.description: No identification of any bias; response is unrelated.
Mentions overconfidence but does not name the specific bias.
Identifies the Dunning‑Kruger effect by name.
Explains why Reed exhibits the Dunning‑Kruger effect, linking her limited experience to inflated confidence.
Provides a nuanced explanation of the asymmetry—how lack of competence prevents recognition of gaps—and suggests a mitigation strategy (e.g., mentorship, deliberate practice).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Ask the player to reconsider Reed's statements: "What evidence from the scene suggests she might be missing critical knowledge?"
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Reward the player with a boost to their Insight skill and unlock a mentorship dialogue with Dr. Havel.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Mara Havel is seasoned, pragmatic, and deeply aware of her own limitations; she values humility and continuous learning.

scenario.context: A ranger patrol of six members is traveling along the Willow Creek trail when a lone traveler trips and falls, drawing the attention of a prowling wolf. The wolf snarls and lunges at the traveler. The other five rangers see the danger but each looks to the others for a cue.
scenario.text: The traveler cries out: "Help! A wolf!" The wolf snaps its jaws shut on the traveler's cloak. Ranger Lira tightens her grip on her spear, but glances at Ranger Joren, who is scanning the trees. Ranger Joren, noticing Lira's hesitation, looks toward Ranger Kade, who is adjusting his pack. Ranger Kade, seeing the others pause, thinks: "Someone else will step in." The wolf, sensing the lack of immediate resistance, backs off briefly, then circles for another attack. No ranger takes decisive action.
scenario.speaker_context: Each ranger justifies inaction by assuming another patrol member will intervene, creating a cascade of collective paralysis.

structure.pattern_description: When multiple observers are present, each individual feels less personal responsibility to act. They look to the behavior of others for social proof; if others do nothing, they interpret the situation as non‑urgent and suppress their own impulse to intervene. This diffusion of responsibility leads to collective inaction even in life‑threatening emergencies.
structure.why_wrong: The presence of many rangers should increase the likelihood of a rescue, but the bystander effect flips that expectation. Responsibility becomes diffused, each ranger assumes someone else will act, and the victim suffers because no one does. The bias turns a potential safety net into a liability.
structure.counterpoint: If one ranger explicitly states a plan—e.g., "I will engage the wolf now"—the diffusion collapses and the others can support the action, breaking the bystander effect.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is illustrated by the rangers' hesitation to act while the wolf attacks the traveler?

rubric.description: No identification or incorrect bias named.
Names a bias but provides an incomplete or inaccurate explanation.
Correctly identifies the Bystander effect but does not explain why it occurs.
Identifies the Bystander effect and explains diffusion of responsibility and social proof.
Fully articulates the Bystander effect, links it to the scenario details, and suggests how to counteract it.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that when several witnesses are present, each tends to assume someone else will intervene, leading to collective inaction. Ask the player to rewrite the scene so one ranger takes the initiative.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the observation and ask the player to describe a concrete step the patrol could take to prevent the bystander effect in future encounters.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Lira is cautious but decisive when she feels personally responsible; Joren is a rule‑follower who waits for orders; Kade is a pragmatic survivor who avoids unnecessary risk.

game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player chooses to have a ranger act, the wolf is driven off, the traveler is rescued, and the patrol gains a reputation for decisive action. If they stay passive, the traveler is injured, and the patrol suffers a morale penalty.

A heavy silence follows. You notice innkeeper Mara shifting in her seat, eyes darting toward the door, but she says nothing. After the meeting, she pulls you aside, whispering, "I tried to point out that a 15% hike will drive customers to the back alleys where they drink illegally. structure.why_wrong: The decision is based on conformity rather than critical analysis, increasing the risk of an economic backlash that could hurt all tavern owners.

scenario.text: "The Crimson Blades' plan is solid," Mara declares, tapping the parchment. "Their scouts have been with us for years, they know the tunnels, they understand our code. It's a trustworthy approach." She flips the page to the Gray Wolves' proposal. "The Gray Wolves' plan looks... adequate. Same timing, same ambush points, same loot split. scenario.speaker_context: Mara is not intentionally deceptive; she genuinely believes the Crimson Blades' plan is superior because she has fought alongside them for years. Her evaluation of the Gray Wolves' plan is colored by in-group favoritism—she grants the familiar group the benefit of the doubt while scrutinizing the out‑group.

structure.pattern_description: In-group bias is the tendency to favor members of one's own group—evaluating their work more charitably, trusting them more readily, and attributing positive qualities to them—while viewing out‑group members with suspicion, scrutiny, and less charitable interpretation. Mara rates the Crimson Blades' identical plan higher than the Gray Wolves' solely because of group affiliation.
structure.formal_form: Agent A belongs to group G. A evaluates work W1 (from G) and W2 (from not‑G). W1 and W2 are objectively equivalent. A rates W1 higher than W2. The difference is attributable to group membership, not to any quality difference in the work.
structure.why_wrong: Mara's judgment is flawed because it ignores objective evidence and relies on loyalty rather than merit. This can lead to suboptimal decisions, wasted resources, and unfair treatment of capable allies, ultimately weakening the hideout's overall effectiveness.
structure.counterpoint: A rational approach would compare the two plans based on concrete criteria—timing, risk, expected loot—ignoring who authored them. If both are truly identical, the decision should be based on random selection or on factors unrelated to group identity, such as who can mobilize troops faster.

scenario.text: Master Ironhelm inspects Joren's sword first. He smiles, recalling Joren's habit of bringing fresh bread for the crew every morning. 'Ah, Joren, you always keep the forge lively. This blade looks fine enough,' he says, noting a slight wobble in the balance but dismissing it. He then turns to Bram's sword. Bram is quiet, rarely speaks, and keeps to himself in the corner. Ironhelm frowns. 'Bram, you never help with the chores. Look at this uneven edge—clearly careless work.' scenario.speaker_context: Master Ironhelm is displaying the halo effect: his positive impression of Joren's friendliness leads him to overlook flaws in Joren's sword, while his negative impression of Bram's aloofness causes him to overemphasize minor imperfections.

structure.pattern_description: The halo effect occurs when an individual's overall impression of a person influences specific judgments about that person, regardless of objective evidence. In this scenario, Ironhelm's affection for Joren causes him to interpret the sword's flaws leniently, while his dislike for Bram leads to harsher criticism of the same level of quality.

structure.counterpoint: Encourage Master Ironhelm to use a standardized checklist that scores each sword on balance, sharpness, and engraving independently of personal feelings.

A murmuring vendor leans in and whispers, "The evidence is identical. Thorn just likes Maren and dislikes Grol. Notice how he frames the facts differently."
scenario.speaker_context: Captain Thorn is demonstrating the halo effect: his favorable view of Maren leads him to interpret ambiguous evidence in her favor, while his unfavorable view of Grol leads him to interpret the same evidence as proof of guilt.

structure.pattern_description: The halo effect is the cognitive bias where a positive impression of someone in one domain influences judgments about them in unrelated domains, and conversely a negative impression leads to harsher judgments. Here, the guard captain's likability of Maren causes him to downplay the evidence, while his dislike of Grol causes him to exaggerate it.
structure.why_wrong: The captain's verdicts are based on his personal feelings toward the merchants, not on an objective analysis of the identical evidence. This bias can lead to unfair outcomes and undermines the integrity of the justice system.
structure.counterpoint: An unbiased adjudicator would evaluate the evidence in the same way for both merchants, leading to consistent verdicts regardless of personal feelings.

scenario.context: In the mining colony of Deepstone, the Council of Overseers meets to decide how to allocate the limited safety budget for the next quarter. Two weeks ago a dramatic tunnel collapse trapped several miners and was covered extensively in the colony's holo‑news. The official incident report shows that, over the past year, equipment thefts from the supply depot have caused far greater material loss than any single collapse.
scenario.text:
Overseer Lira steps to the podium. "You all saw the tunnel collapse on the western shaft. Six miners were buried, three barely escaped, and the whole colony has been on edge. I propose we divert half of our safety budget to reinforce all western tunnels and hire extra rescue crews, even if it means cutting back on the supply depot's anti‑theft upgrades." 

Chief Engineer Harn raises his tablet. "The data shows we've had twelve theft incidents in the past six months, each costing us roughly five hundred ore units. The collapse cost us only two hundred ore units in lost equipment, and no lives were lost thanks to the emergency protocols. If we keep the anti‑theft measures, we could prevent a loss of three thousand ore units this quarter." 

Lira shakes her head. "Numbers are cold, Harn. The faces of those trapped are still fresh. The miners need to feel safe, not worry about missing tools. Fear is a powerful motivator."
scenario.speaker_context: Overseer Lira is a well‑meaning leader who wants the colonists to feel secure, but her decision is being driven by the vivid, recent tunnel collapse rather than the statistically larger, ongoing threat of equipment theft.

structure.pattern_description: Lira judges the severity and likelihood of future incidents based on how easily the recent tunnel collapse comes to mind, ignoring the higher base rate and cumulative impact of frequent thefts. The vivid, emotional memory of the collapse skews her risk assessment and leads to a suboptimal allocation of limited safety resources.
structure.formal_form: Agent judges frequency or probability of event type E based on the ease with which instances of E come to mind, rather than on actual base rates. Vivid, recent, or emotionally charged events are over‑weighted.
structure.why_wrong: Lira overestimates the future risk of collapses because the incident is recent and emotionally salient, while underestimating the steady, larger loss from thefts. This misallocation could leave the depot vulnerable and waste resources that would better protect overall colony productivity.
structure.counterpoint: A rational approach would weigh both the probability and impact of each threat using the colony's incident logs, allocating resources proportionally to the expected loss rather than to the most emotionally vivid event.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Overseer Lira displaying when she prioritizes tunnel reinforcement over anti‑theft measures?

Mentions a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., confirmation bias).
Identifies the availability heuristic but cannot explain why it applies.
Correctly names the availability heuristic and gives a brief explanation linking vividness of the collapse to the decision.
Fully articulates the availability heuristic, contrasts it with base‑rate reasoning, and connects the explanation to the specific dialogue and data presented.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Review the section on "How vivid events skew risk perception" and compare the collapse incident with the theft statistics to see which factor is more readily recalled.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! Now consider how you would redesign the budget proposal to incorporate both the emotional impact of the collapse and the statistical threat of theft.

scenario.context: The player has joined a traveling theater troupe that must choose its next performance to attract a wealthy patron. Two senior members present the same play, but each describes it with a different emotional frame.
scenario.text: Director Mira steps forward: "Our new piece celebrates the courage of 150 villagers who survived the flood—it's a triumphant story of hope. I think we should showcase it to the patron tomorrow." Stagehand Dorian counters: "That same script recounts how 150 villagers lost everything in the flood—it's a tragic tale of sorrow. Presenting it now would only dampen the patron's mood. We should pick a lighter comedy instead." The troupe's manager, Lila, looks puzzled: "Are you both talking about the same play?" Mira and Dorian glance at each other, realizing they are. The only difference is the framing—"triumph" versus "tragedy"—which is steering their recommendations.
scenario.speaker_context: This mirrors the classic framing effect: identical factual content (the fate of 150 villagers) is presented as a gain (survival, hope) or a loss (destruction, sorrow). The emotional framing changes the troupe's perceived desirability of the performance, even though the underlying story is unchanged.

structure.pattern_description: The framing effect occurs when the way information is presented influences judgment and decision-making, despite the underlying facts being identical. In the troupe, the same play is described as a story of triumph (gain frame) or as a story of tragedy (loss frame). The gain frame leads the director to recommend the play, while the loss frame leads the stagehand to reject it. The bias lies in reacting to the presentation rather than the content.
structure.formal_form: Given factual outcome F (e.g., 150 villagers survive), it can be expressed as gain G ('150 survived') or loss L ('150 perished'). Agent exposed to G evaluates F positively; agent exposed to L evaluates F negatively. Decision D changes based solely on frame, not on F.
structure.why_wrong: Rational decision‑making should be based on the actual consequences, not on whether those consequences are described as gains or losses. The troupe members are allowing the emotional framing to dictate their recommendation, which can lead to suboptimal choices such as rejecting a potentially profitable performance.
structure.counterpoint: A more balanced approach would restate the facts neutrally—"The play depicts the fate of 150 villagers during a flood"—allowing the troupe to evaluate the artistic and financial merits without the bias introduced by gain or loss framing.

assessment.identification_prompt: After listening to Mira and Dorian, identify the cognitive bias influencing their opposite recommendations and explain why it leads to a faulty decision.

rubric.description: No identification of any bias; response is unrelated.
Mentions a bias but mislabels it (e.g., calls it "optimism bias").
Correctly names the framing effect but provides an incomplete explanation of why it matters.
Accurately names the framing effect and explains how the gain vs. loss wording skews judgments.
Provides a thorough explanation, cites the neutral restatement as a corrective, and connects the bias to potential real‑world consequences for the troupe.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The NPC mentor, Master Arlen, says: "Notice how the same story is painted in two lights. When you see that, you’ll recognize the framing effect and can strip away the bias before deciding."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Master Arlen nods approvingly: "Exactly. By reframing the information neutrally, the troupe can make a decision based on the play’s true merit rather than emotional wording."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mira is passionate, optimistic, and tends to see the bright side; Dorian is pragmatic, cautious, and often focuses on potential downsides.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Mira: "Imagine the applause when we celebrate hope!" Dorian: "Imagine the silence when we remind them of loss..."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can suggest a neutral summary of the play’s plot, prompting both Mira and Dorian to reassess their positions and reach a consensus based on audience interest and patron preferences rather than framing.

scenario.context: The traveling troupe "Silver Lantern" is preparing for a high‑stakes performance in the city of Valoria. Before each rehearsal, the troupe's stage manager, Maribel, hands each actor a small vial of "Elixir of Focus" – a warm infusion of rosemary and honey. Maribel swears by the brew, saying it steadies nerves and sharpens memory. The actors, believing in its power, report feeling calmer and delivering more confident lines. The troupe's director, Maestro Lucien, a skeptic of superstitions, has just arrived and is uneasy about the reliance on the mysterious potion.
scenario.text:
"Your actors are performing better than ever," Maribel says, holding up a vial. "The Elixir of Focus clears the mind and steadies the heart. Trust the brew, and the stage will be yours." 

Lucien frowns. "I've observed their rehearsals. I see no difference in the script or lighting. What exactly is in that mixture?" 

Maribel smiles. "Just rosemary, honey, and hot water. Nothing magical. Yet every actor who drinks it claims the tremor fades, the words flow. If I told a lead actress that the brew does nothing, would she still rise without a quaver? The belief is the catalyst."
scenario.speaker_context: Maribel demonstrates the placebo effect: she gives a harmless herbal infusion, tells the actors it will improve performance, and they indeed improve because of expectation. Lucien represents evidence‑based thinking, questioning whether the improvement is truly due to the brew or the actors' belief.

structure.pattern_description: The placebo effect occurs when a person experiences real improvement in symptoms or performance because they expect a treatment to work, even though the treatment has no active therapeutic component. It is considered a dual pattern because the effect is genuine (belief produces measurable change) yet can mislead observers into attributing the change to the treatment itself rather than to expectation.
structure.formal_form: If an individual receives a neutral intervention T, believes T is effective, then the individual's condition C improves. The causal chain is: belief → physiological/psychological response → improvement, not T → improvement.
structure.why_wrong: Assuming the Elixir contains a magical or pharmacological property leads to a false attribution of cause, obscuring the true source of improvement and potentially discouraging the development of legitimate techniques for stage confidence.
structure.why_right: Recognizing that the actors' belief in the Elixir is what drives their enhanced performance acknowledges the power of expectation, allowing the troupe to harness psychological preparation ethically without relying on deception.
structure.counterpoint: Lucien argues that relying on a placebo, even a benign one, can be ethically questionable because it involves deception. He suggests teaching actors concrete breathing and visualization techniques instead of a mysterious brew.

assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You’ve spotted the Placebo effect. Think about how the troupe could use this knowledge responsibly—perhaps by teaching confidence‑building routines that rely on expectation rather than secret brews.

scenario.text: A scream echoes: "Help! He's bleeding!" The injured villager clutches his side, blood soaking the stone. Around him, twenty onlookers pause.
